foods.name: Sugar
foods.summary: Rots teeth, adds easy kilojoules, and the sugar industry spent decades steering science away from it.

told.text: "Just empty calories. Fat is the real problem."

evidence.text: A proven cause of tooth decay and a contributor to weight gain, especially in drinks.

science.text: The WHO says keep "free" sugars (added sugar plus honey, syrups and juice) under 10% of energy, ideally under 5%. That's about 25 g, or 6 teaspoons, a day for an adult.
Tooth decay rises with sugar intake at every level studied. This is the strongest evidence.
Eating more sugar raises body weight. Swapping sugar for the same kilojoules of starch does not, so the problem is the extra energy.
In a large US cohort, people getting 25% or more of their calories from added sugar had nearly three times the risk of dying of heart disease. That is observational evidence, not proof of cause.

sources.label: Yang et al., JAMA Intern Med 2014

foods.australia: Australia has no sugar tax. The 2016 Grattan Institute proposal for a sugary drinks tax was rejected. The University of Sydney's "Australian Paradox" paper (2011), which claimed Australians were eating less sugar while getting fatter, needed corrections and drew years of criticism.
foods.what_to_do: Worry most about sugar you drink. A little in food is fine; a can of soft drink alone is about 10 teaspoons.

foods.name: Soft drinks
foods.summary: The single clearest diet–disease link in nutrition, and the most heavily defended product.

told.text: "Fine as part of an active lifestyle. The problem is lack of exercise."

evidence.text: Strongly linked to weight gain, type 2 diabetes and tooth decay.

science.text: One sugary drink a day was linked to an 18% higher risk of type 2 diabetes (13% after allowing for body weight).
Trials and cohort studies show sugary drinks cause weight gain in children and adults.

sources.label: Malik et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2013

science.text: Two or more a day was linked to a higher risk of early death in two big US cohorts.
Taxes work: Mexico's 2014 tax cut purchases by 6% in the first year and 12% by the end of it. The UK levy pushed makers to cut sugar and was linked to 8% fewer obese 10–11-year-old girls.

foods.australia: In Australia a 375 ml can of regular cola holds about 40 g of sugar, about 10 teaspoons. There's no tax; the industry instead pledged a voluntary 20% sugar cut.
foods.what_to_do: Water, or diet versions if you need the fizz. A 600 ml bottle a day adds up to about 23 kg of sugar a year.

foods.name: Fruit juice
foods.summary: Sold as a serve of fruit; for your teeth and your blood sugar it behaves more like soft drink.

told.text: "A healthy glass of fruit. Nothing added."

evidence.text: The sugar counts as "free sugar". Small links to weight gain; whole fruit is better.

science.text: The WHO counts the sugars in juice as free sugars, the same category as added sugar.
Each daily serve of 100% juice was linked to slightly higher BMI in children, and about 0.2 kg extra weight in adults.
Whole fruit was linked to a lower risk of type 2 diabetes; fruit juice to a higher one.
Australia's guidelines count juice as fruit only "occasionally", and only 125 ml.

foods.australia: Juice was exempt from the UK sugar levy. The researchers suggested that may be one reason it didn't help younger children.
foods.what_to_do: Eat the orange, don't drink three. If you like juice, keep it to a small glass.

foods.name: Artificial sweeteners
foods.summary: Better than sugar for your teeth, no help for long-term weight, and the cancer scare is mostly noise.

told.text: "Zero sugar, so it helps you lose weight."

evidence.text: Safe at normal intakes, but no proven long-term benefit for weight. Some open questions.

science.text: The WHO (2023) advises against using sweeteners for weight control: no long-term benefit for body fat, and a possible (low-certainty) link to diabetes and heart disease.
IARC called aspartame "possibly carcinogenic" (Group 2B, limited evidence). The same WHO review kept the safe daily limit, which is about 9–14 cans of diet drink a day for a 70 kg adult.
Higher blood erythritol was linked to heart attack and stroke, and erythritol made blood platelets stickier. It is early evidence, but worth watching.

foods.australia: Most Australian "no sugar" soft drinks use aspartame, sucralose, acesulfame or stevia.
foods.what_to_do: Swapping regular soft drink for diet is a step up. Swapping it for water is a bigger one.

foods.name: Ultra-processed food
foods.summary: The strongest new idea in nutrition, with a real trial behind it, but a blunt category that lumps bread with lollies.

told.text: "A calorie is a calorie. There are no bad foods, only bad diets."

evidence.text: Diets high in UPF make people overeat and are linked to many diseases, though not every UPF is equal.

science.text: In a tightly controlled NIH trial, people on an ultra-processed diet ate about 500 more calories a day and gained 0.9 kg in two weeks.
A 2024 review of studies covering about 10 million people linked high UPF intake to 32 health problems, including cardiovascular death (+50%), type 2 diabetes and depression.
Not all UPF behaves alike: processed meats and sugary drinks drive most of the risk, while wholegrain breads and cereals often show none.

sources.label: Cordova et al., Lancet Reg Health Europe 2023

science.text: A 2025 Lancet series by 43 experts said UPF makers block regulation with the same tactics as tobacco. Critics note most of the evidence is observational.

sources.label: Lancet series on ultra-processed food, Nov 2025 (CNN report)

foods.australia: About 42% of the energy Australians eat comes from ultra-processed food (Machado et al., BMJ Open 2019, using the 2011–12 national survey). San Francisco's 2025 lawsuit against ten UPF makers is being watched closely here.
foods.what_to_do: Don't panic about every packet. Cut back on the obvious ones: soft drinks, processed meat, sweets, chips and fast food.

foods.name: Alcohol
foods.summary: The "glass of red is good for your heart" story fell apart; the cancer link didn't.

told.text: "A drink a day keeps the cardiologist away."

evidence.text: A Group 1 carcinogen. Less is better; the heart "benefit" was mostly a statistical illusion.

science.text: Alcohol causes at least seven cancers, including breast and bowel. The WHO says no safe level has been identified.
Breast cancer risk rises about 7% for each 10 g a day, which is one Australian standard drink. Bowel cancer risk also rises about 7%.
Once studies stopped comparing drinkers with "sick quitters" (people who gave up because they were ill), the apparent benefit of light drinking disappeared.

sources.label: Zhao et al., JAMA Network Open 2023

science.text: The US Surgeon General (2025) called for cancer warnings on alcohol labels.

foods.australia: Australia's guideline: no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any day (NHMRC 2020). Pregnancy warnings became compulsory in 2023, after the industry fought the red label.
foods.what_to_do: Fewer is better, and alcohol-free days help. Try the drinks counter in "Try it yourself" below.

foods.name: Red & processed meat
foods.summary: Processed meat is a proven bowel-cancer cause; red meat is a "probably", and both are linked to diabetes.

told.text: "Keep eating it. The evidence against meat is weak."

evidence.text: Processed meat raises bowel cancer risk; red meat probably does; both linked to type 2 diabetes.

science.text: IARC: processed meat causes bowel cancer (Group 1; +18% per 50 g a day, about two slices of ham). Red meat probably does (Group 2A; +17% per 100 g a day).
Across 1.97 million people, 50 g a day of processed meat was linked to 15% more type 2 diabetes, and 100 g of unprocessed red meat to 10% more.

sources.label: Li et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2024

science.text: Processed meat, but not unprocessed red meat, was linked to more heart disease.
"Group 1" means the evidence is as certain as for tobacco, not that the harm is as big. Smoking multiplies lung cancer risk 15–30 times; processed meat raises bowel cancer risk by about a fifth.

foods.australia: Cancer Council Australia: limit lean red meat to 455 g cooked a week and keep processed meat to a minimum.
foods.what_to_do: Make ham and bacon occasional. Red meat a few times a week is fine within 455 g.

foods.name: Eggs
foods.summary: Off the naughty list for most people. But the egg industry paid for a lot of that rehabilitation.

told.text: "A cholesterol bomb. No more than 3 a week."

evidence.text: Up to an egg a day shows no clear link to heart disease for most people.

science.text: Pooled data on 1.7 million people found no link between up to an egg a day and heart disease.
But in six other US cohorts, each extra half-egg a day was linked to a 6% higher risk of heart disease, so the debate isn't over.
The Heart Foundation (2019) dropped its egg limit for healthy people, but suggests fewer than 7 a week for people with type 2 diabetes.

sources.label: Heart Foundation advice on eggs, 2019 (MJA InSight)

science.text: An analysis by a vegan advocacy group found industry funding of egg–cholesterol studies rose from 0% in the 1950s to 60% in the 2010s.

sources.label: Barnard et al., Am J Lifestyle Med 2019

foods.australia: The ACCC won penalties against egg farms whose "free range" hens barely went outside. The 2017 national standard then allowed up to 10,000 hens per hectare.
foods.what_to_do: An egg a day is fine for most people. What comes with it (bacon, butter, white toast) matters more.

foods.name: Milk & dairy
foods.summary: Neither the miracle the ads promised nor the poison its critics claim. Yoghurt looks best.

told.text: "Strong bones! Three serves a day helps you lose weight."

evidence.text: Fine for most people; probably lowers bowel cancer risk. No weight-loss magic, and little sign it prevents fractures.

science.text: Drinking more milk was not linked to fewer hip fractures in women.

sources.label: Bischoff-Ferrari et al., J Bone Miner Res 2011

science.text: Dairy probably lowers bowel cancer risk (World Cancer Research Fund). High intakes may slightly raise prostate cancer risk (limited evidence).
Yoghurt is consistently linked to lower type 2 diabetes risk.
Dairy, including full-fat, was linked to lower death and heart disease rates across 21 countries.

foods.australia: Selling raw milk for drinking is illegal in Australia. A Victorian toddler died in 2014 after drinking raw "bath milk".
foods.what_to_do: Enjoy it if you like it. Plain yoghurt is a good choice; flavoured milk is mainly a sugar drink.

foods.name: Seed oils
foods.summary: The internet's favourite villain. The evidence says swapping butter for these oils protects your heart.

told.text: "Toxic, inflammatory industrial sludge. Cook in tallow."

evidence.text: Replacing saturated fat with these oils lowers LDL and heart disease risk.

science.text: Cutting saturated fat for two years or more reduced heart attacks and strokes, most when it was replaced with polyunsaturated oils.
Across 30 cohorts, people with the most linoleic acid (the main omega-6 in seed oils) in their blood had a lower risk of heart disease death.
Among 221,000 people followed for 33 years, butter eaters died earlier and plant-oil users lived longer.

sources.label: Zhang et al., JAMA Intern Med 2025

science.text: Trials don't show that eating linoleic acid raises inflammation markers, the core claim of the "seed oils are inflammatory" theory.

sources.label: Johnson & Fritsche, J Acad Nutr Diet 2012

foods.australia: The best evidence against seed oils is Australian: the Sydney Diet Heart Study (1966–73), whose full data only came out in 2013. See the case list.
foods.what_to_do: Olive oil is the best-studied choice. Canola and sunflower are fine too. Deep-frying anything, in any fat, is the real problem.

foods.name: Butter & saturated fat
foods.summary: "Butter is back" made headlines in 2014. It never really came back.

told.text: "Eat butter. Coconut oil is a superfood."

evidence.text: Raises LDL cholesterol; swapping it for unsaturated oils lowers heart risk.

science.text: The American Heart Association found that replacing saturated with polyunsaturated fat cut heart disease by about 30% in trials.
Coconut oil raised LDL cholesterol compared with plant oils in trials.
More butter was linked to 15% higher death rates over 33 years.

sources.label: Zhang et al., JAMA Intern Med 2025

science.text: The food matters: saturated fat in cheese and yoghurt seems less harmful than in butter or fatty meat.

foods.australia: Coconut oil was a 2010s supermarket craze in Australia too. Australia never banned trans fats outright; levels here are low by voluntary reformulation.
foods.what_to_do: Use olive or canola oil for most cooking. Keep butter and coconut oil for taste, not health.

foods.name: Salt
foods.summary: A huge trial led from Sydney went a long way to settling the "salt wars": less sodium means fewer strokes.

told.text: "Salt is harmless, and low-salt diets are dangerous."

evidence.text: Too much raises blood pressure; cutting it, or swapping to potassium salt, prevents strokes.

science.text: In a five-year trial of 20,995 people, swapping salt for a potassium salt substitute cut strokes by 14% and deaths by 12%.
The WHO recommends under 5 g of salt a day. The world average is about 10.8 g.

foods.australia: The salt substitute trial (SSaSS) was led by Sydney's George Institute and funded by the NHMRC. Most salt Australians eat comes from bread, processed meat and takeaway, not the shaker.
foods.what_to_do: If you have high blood pressure, ask your GP about potassium salt substitutes. Most people with kidney disease shouldn't use them.

foods.name: Baby formula
foods.summary: Formula is safe and vital for many babies. The marketing, and some factories, are the problem.

told.text: "Closer than ever to breast milk. Boosts brain development."

evidence.text: A safe substitute when needed. Most "brain" and "immunity" claims lack good evidence; toddler milks are unnecessary.

science.text: A 2023 Lancet series found that the US$55 billion formula industry uses marketing that exploits parents' worries, with health claims that lack good evidence.

sources.label: Lancet series on breastfeeding and formula marketing, 2023

science.text: The 1981 WHO marketing code bans promoting formula to parents. Most countries only partly enforce it.

sources.label: Lancet series on breastfeeding and formula marketing, 2023

foods.australia: Australia's formula marketing agreement (MAIF) is voluntary, and it doesn't cover toddler milks, which are heavily advertised.
foods.what_to_do: Fed is best. If you use formula, a basic standard formula is as good as a premium one. Toddlers over 12 months don't need toddler milk.

foods.name: Cereal & "healthy" snacks
foods.summary: The home of the health halo: stars, ticks and claims printed on boxes of sugar.

told.text: "Part of a healthy breakfast. Improves attentiveness. Supports immunity."

evidence.text: High-fibre wholegrain cereals are good; many kids' cereals and snacks are a quarter to two-thirds sugar.

science.text: Higher fibre and wholegrain intakes are linked to 15–30% less heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and bowel cancer.
The FTC found Kellogg's "improves attentiveness by nearly 20%" claim was false. The company's own study didn't show it.

foods.australia: Milo carried 4.5 Health Stars because it was rated as if made with skim milk; on its own the powder scored 1.5. Only 13% of people drank it that way.
foods.what_to_do: Check the fibre and the sugar, not the stars. Plain oats, muesli without added sugar, or wholegrain biscuits.

foods.name: Coffee & tea
foods.summary: Once suspected of causing heart disease and cancer, now one of the most consistently "protective" drinks.

told.text: "Bad for your heart, and possibly carcinogenic."

evidence.text: 3–4 cups a day is linked to lower death rates, less liver disease and less type 2 diabetes.

science.text: A review of 200+ meta-analyses found 3–4 cups a day linked to the lowest risk of death, heart disease and liver cancer. Caution in pregnancy.
IARC removed coffee from its "possibly carcinogenic" list in 2016. Only very hot drinks (over about 65 °C) are flagged.

foods.australia: Australia's café culture runs on milk-based coffee. The milk doesn't cancel the benefits; the syrups and sugar can.
foods.what_to_do: Enjoy it. Avoid too much late in the day, and go easy if you're pregnant.

Heart & stroke.note: Linked to more heart disease in cohorts.

Bowel cancer.note: Some links via obesity; no direct case.

Weight gain.note: More sugar means more kilojoules (Te Morenga 2013).

Teeth.note: The main dietary cause of tooth decay.

Early death.note: Hard to separate from the rest of the diet.

Weight gain.note: Small gains in children and adults.

Heart & stroke.note: Possible links in cohorts (low certainty); erythritol under study.

Type 2 diabetes.note: Cohort links may reflect people already at risk.

Weight gain.note: Trial: +500 kcal a day, +0.9 kg in 2 weeks.

Heart & stroke.note: Raises blood pressure, atrial fibrillation and stroke risk; the "protective" effect looks like bias.

Early death.note: Risk rises with amount; light drinking shows no benefit once bias is removed.

Heart & stroke.note: +42% heart disease per 50 g a day (Micha 2010).

Bowel cancer.note: IARC Group 1: +18% per 50 g a day.

Heart & stroke.note: Up to 1 a day: no clear link in most analyses.

Type 2 diabetes.note: US studies suggest risk; others don’t.

Other cancers.note: Possibly higher prostate risk at high intakes.

Heart & stroke.note: Lower heart disease when replacing saturated fat.

Type 2 diabetes.note: Higher linoleic acid, lower diabetes risk.

Early death.note: Plant oils linked to lower mortality.
800 g a day linked to 31% lower early death (Aune 2017).
